The radar cross section (RCS) of an object is a crucial parameter in a wide range of applications, including military and civilian applications.
Reverberation chambers (RCs) have become a promising alternative testing facility for a wide range of electromagnetic applications, including RCS measurement.

The method proposed in this paper involves a two-step process: 1) Measure the reflection coefficient of the antenna oriented towards the target, and 2) Measure the same reflection coefficient without the target present.
The distance between the antenna and the target was 2.95 m, which is large enough so that the ballistic wave can be considered a plane wave at the target position.
The measurements were performed in the 9.75 GHz - 10.25 GHz frequency range, which is very high compared to the RC's Lowest Useable Frequency (around 200 MHz).
The RCS pattern of a metallic plate was evaluated over the azimuthal angle range of -30° to 30° with an angular step of 1 degree.
The horn antenna used in the experiments was vertically polarized with an electric field along the height of the RC.
The authors show that the RCS pattern accuracy strongly depends on the choice of the stirrer position when computing the difference between the two measurements (with and without the target).

The error in the RCS pattern remains low at low stirrer position shifts (below 20 degrees), but the results become less reliable at higher shifts, and a shift of 36 degrees makes it impossible to extract the RCS.
The theoretical RCS of the metallic plate is calculated using the expression σ = 4πS^2/c^2, where S is the target section and c is the speed of light.
Contrary to the method proposed in [7], the method in this paper does not require any time gating, thus avoiding the need for Fourier Transform.
The authors recommend that the same stirrer position should be chosen for the two measurements (with and without the target) in order to increase the RCS pattern estimation accuracy.

The results obtained in the reverberation chamber for a fixed stirrer position (θ_st = 0°) showed good agreement with the reference measurement in an anechoic chamber, except for the lowest levels of RCS.

The reverberation chamber can be proposed as a valid and economically convenient alternative to the well-established anechoic chamber for RCS measurements of canonical targets, with some carefulness regarding the stirrer position.
